utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, Dr. Subotic. Are there any matters to raise? Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the testimony of Mr. Zecevic, I would like to first ask the Chamber to -- or at least call to the Chamber's attention a dispute that the Prosecution and we are having, in which we couldn't seem to resolve among ourselves, concerning which parts of his testimony are expert testimony and which parts are factual testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are going to raise that issue, we are informed of it in brief manner and we are going to give a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Then I won't say more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Before the witness is brought in, we will deal with it, concerning this evidence. As you are aware, the Chamber previously ordered that Dr. Zecevic to be brought as a viva voce witness rather than pursuant to Rule 92 ter. However, we then observed that in the notification filed by the Prosecution, a statement provided by the witness in 2008 is listed as an expert report, to be tendered as such. Having reviewed the content of this statement, and being cognizant of the fact that Mr. Robinson has already communicated his objection to its admission as an expert report, the Chamber is of the view that it is not appropriate for the statement to be tendered as an expert report. Indeed, its content is of a factual nature concerning matters which Dr. Zecevic observed and experienced during his previous employment. So Mr. Gaynor, if you intend for any of this material to be put into evidence, it should be led live from the witness. Second, I believe, Mr. Robinson, that you also have an objection to the admission of the report titled, "Study of the circumstances and causes of the massacre at the Markale market on 5th of February, 1994," as an expert report. However, having reviewed the content of the report, the Chamber considers that it was prepared by Dr. Zecevic and others as experts in the field of ballistics, and to give their expert opinion on the Markale I incident. We are therefore satisfied that it is appropriately characterised as an expert report rather than as a factual report akin to some of the police reports previously admitted in this case. Now, Mr. Gaynor, I hope that you anticipated that you may have to lead the evidence that was in the 2008 statement as live evidence and that you are ready to commence your examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready to commence my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is a few further matters. Probably as everyone is aware, due to Dr. Zecevic's medical condition, we are sitting today on a slightly altered schedule with more frequent short breaks. Although we are already ten minutes or five minutes into the session, I'd like to stick to the anticipated schedule, which the parties are all aware of and we will have a five-minutes break at 2.40. During the break, if everyone could please remain in the courtroom while we judges withdraw and Dr. Zecevic may stand up and move around a little. I would appreciate everyone's cooperation in ensuring that breaks take no more than five minutes. And should it be discussed in the presence of the witness? But I was advised that the parties are happy to have a hearing in the morning tomorrow, given that there will be a hearing in the afternoon in this courtroom. And Thursday and Friday, would it be okay to have hearing from 1.30 to 7 in a somewhat extended format with three 90-minute sessions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's fine, as far as we are concerned, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That said, we will bring in the witness. Of course, we will sit in regular times tomorrow, i.e. from 9.30 to 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor, if you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whenever you find it uncomfortable, Dr. Zecevic, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to ask if I can occasionally stand up without prior announcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Dr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you begin, Dr. Zecevic, I appreciate very much your cooperation with the Tribunal in that you have agreed to testify as long as necessary, although it was your position that you wanted to testify only for three hours. At this moment, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that Mr. Karadzic has a fundamental right to cross-examine any of the witnesses against him, so it is particularly so given that he's charged with very serious criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am at your disposal for as long as you see fit that I need to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Berko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Zecevic, unless there is an objection, I'm going to go through a few aspects of your professional and work background, and academic background. I'll be grateful if you could just confirm those for me. From August 1975 until 1992, you worked at the Pretis factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That factory produced artillery and rocket ammunition and aircraft bombs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You worked in the research and development centre and your primary fields of work were rocket motors and war heads and developing new rocket projectiles?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: During your 17 years at Pretis, you became familiar with documentation issued to, and received by, Pretis relating to the manufacture and delivery of ammunition and weapons?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Simultaneously, while you were working at Pretis, since 1976, you've been a member of the faculty at Sarajevo University's Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, first in the mechanics department and later in the department of defence technology?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You're currently the head of the defence technology department at the mechanical engineering faculty at the university of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Between 1980 and today, you've published over 50 academic papers and several books in several different areas of ballistics?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to tell the Court, specifically in respect of the 120-millimetre mortar unit used by the VRS, what is your familiarity with that specific mortar unit?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the projectile?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, very well, the projectile.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with it because my factory also produced 120-millimetre mortar projectile and then later that manufacture was transferred to a facility in Croatia. Licki Osik and it was my task to develop the propaganda 120-millimetre mine. This is a mine aimed at reducing the morale of enemy forces and the basis for such a new projectile was the 120-millimetre mortar projectile. So I'm completely familiar with all the elements of the manufacture of the 120-millimetre mortar projectiles, with its characteristics, and so on. Should I explain anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No. That's fine. I was just waiting on the interpretation. Thank you. Could you tell Their Honours your specific expertise in relation to the modified air-bombs that you've described in one of your expert reports, just in a couple of sentences?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, I had the opportunity to see the fuel segment. This is four rocket missiles and the rocket subsystem, which on that day, I think this was the 29th of January 1994, was fired at the Zuc area, which is a hill above Sarajevo. I was asked to look at it and to try to identify that piece of equipment. Before the war, I was following the International Defence Review magazine and I was looking at the aerosol bomb range of products. In 1995 the use of such systems against Sarajevo intensified and a number of such rocket adapted projectiles fell some 500 metres away from my house. I was interested to see what this device was and if it directly threatened the security of my family, my friends in the neighbourhood where I lived. I was more involved in this area when the judge asked me to try to identify the type of projectile that hit the TV station in Sarajevo, and together with two of my colleagues, I drafted a study on this. After that, the Prosecution in the case of General Milosevic also engaged me to draft a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, prior to the conflict, could you briefly describe your familiarity with air-bombs and specifically fuel-air air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My best friend, Colonel Vladan Tomic, in the Pretis factory was the chief of development of the aerosol bomb, the air-bomb. The two of us spent 15 years together in Pretis because he left Pretis a couple of years before the war began; he went to Belgrade. We lived together nearby. We spent time in each other's company. He was an exceptional expert. We exchanged experiences. I had the opportunity to go with him to Vinca, this is the nuclear institute, and we visited Dr. Zoran Maksimovic there, who was in charge of creating the fuels for aerosol explosions, and who before that specialised in the United States. At that time, I was doing my postgraduate studies and he proposed, Dr. Maksimovic, suggested to me that he be my mentor and that one of the topics of my thesis would be the increase of the efficacy in the application of aerosol bombs. We carried out some experiments in Sarajevo at the practice range of the Pretis factory. Unfortunately, the experiments or the tests were not promising so I abandoned that particular topic for my thesis. This is just a brief summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that in 1992, and 1993, you worked for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you give the dates of your work for the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that on the 10th of April, when intense attacks and provocations began in Sarajevo, I signed up with the Territorial Defence. I became more involved on my own initiative, with students from the mechanical engineering faculty, and with another group, we tried to organise the production of the barest possible war technology in war conditions. Within a month, this group of ours, which was a group of volunteers, merged with another group that was already formed by the Main Staff under the direction of Faik Kulovic, and these two groups merged and created the centre for special purpose industry or the military industry. It was our task to try, in spite of restrictions of electricity, to provide a way, despite of these power cuts, in Sarajevo to produce rocket-launched projectiles and hand grenades. This was our main activity. Since there was no supply of explosive materiel to Sarajevo, because there was a very strong encirclement around Sarajevo, I launched an initiative to use unexploded projectiles that were found, and to extract a certain minimum quantity of explosives, for example, one kilogram of explosives in an unexploded projectile that came from outside of Sarajevo, which struck Sarajevo, that a person who brought in such a projectile would be given 1 hand grenade or one rifle grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just generally speaking, could I request that you keep your answers just a little shorter, then I can ask you for further details as they arise, I'm grateful for your cooperation. I'd like you just to confirm the end date of your service with the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In mid-July 1993, the unit that I was in was dismantled, disbanded, and this transition period from the point in time to disband the unit up until the point of time when this was handed over, which was in September 1993, then from September to December 1993, I was available to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina without any particular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your answer concerning the collection of unexploded projectiles, I want to ask you a very specific question about that. Did you ever pick up or retrieve a 120-millimetre mortar projectile which had not exploded and if so, were you able to use the stabiliser which was on that projectile?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I remember well that I only managed to get at one time a 120-millimetre mortar smoke projectile but I never had any need to use the stabiliser from that projectile because my entire activity had to do with rifle grenades and hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, from -- on the basis of your expert knowledge, could you describe whether it is likely that one might be able to retrieve the stabiliser from a 120-millimetre mortar projectile which had ricochetted and landed without exploding?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, this is possible. In real terms, any projectile, when it ricochets, is exposed to a lot of deviation and is deformed. So nobody would think of taking a part from a used projectile and putting it into a weapon and firing it because that would increase the possibility of an explosion in the barrel during the launching phase rather than actually a successful launch of that projectile at the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, we need to have a break for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 2.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the Pretis factory in Vogosca. Could you explain, in a couple of sentences, the relative importance of the Pretis factory to the entire defence industry within the SFRY prior to the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Pretis factory was an excellent factory, perhaps one of the biggest factories in Europe which produced rocket and other missiles. Its designed capacity was around 750.000 missiles of calibre ranging from 76 to 105 millimetres and realistically from 1986 until 1990, it produced around 350.000 rounds of artillery and rocket projectiles per annum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was part of its production destined for the export market?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately 60 per cent of the output was intended for export and 35 to 40 per cent was intended for the use of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to know why such a significant ammunition facility was located in Bosnia rather than, for example, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the idea was created to develop a military industry within the federal and later on Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, the trend was that in the central part of Yugoslavia, factories would be established that would be capable regardless of whether any invasion came by the USSR or by NATO, to have good capacities for defence of Yugoslavia. In line with that, the majority of factories were based in Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Was it the practice at Pretis to stock raw materials for the manufacture of munitions?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The practice was, and also an obligation, that one segment of the production should be dedicated to parts, without assembling them. The purpose was to have them assembled later on based on logistical needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you able to give an estimate as to the stocks of raw materials held at Pretis in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is not my estimate. This is an estimate of a technological expert who dealt with it. We had an approximately one-year stock of raw materials, and I am referring to metal parts, which were intended for some 350 to 400.000 projectiles on an annual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the day that you stopped working at Pretis. Do you remember what day that was?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do remember. That was a sad day for me. That was the 17th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court why you stopped working there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the period immediately before that date, the situation was extremely tense. There were barricades in Sarajevo, and at one point it seemed that reason would prevail. A number of people who worked at Pretis started coming to work, and I was among them. I remember that on that day, there were about one-third of the currently available people and personnel who came to work. In the building where I worked, which was the development department, were some 15 or 20 of us. I was completely alone in my section because none of my fellow workers appeared. While I was sitting there and doing some work, I felt at one moment an eerie silence. In order for you to grasp how Pretis operated we had a series of plants and about 10.000 people would come to work every day and machines were working all the time, and the sound of machines was actually part of my life. Suddenly, I heard that the machines were silent. I looked out of the window and I saw people leaving the factory in groups. I called the gate house to ask what it was all about, and I was told that quite simply everybody was leaving. So, an extremely negative atmosphere was created. I just picked up a number of books of mine, some research papers that I had, and, believing that this interregnum would probably last 15 to 20 days, I thought that I could continue my work at home. Once I left, I wasn't able to come back to this factory until February of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why, in a sentence, were you not able to come back until February 1996?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because the roads were blocked. There were barricades erected on the roads. Shooting started. I heard on TV that the Yugoslav People's Army, as it was still called, entered the factory. I called Radomir Ecimovic, who was the manager of the development department and I wanted to ask him -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just going to ask you -- I'm grateful for the detail. Could I just focus on whether the factory fell under the control of one party to the conflict or another?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: People couldn't move freely and come to the factory, they were prevented from doing that. Only officers of the JNA were able to come and people, so to speak, of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So were people who were not of Serb ethnicity permitted to work at Pretis after April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to reach the premises of Pretis, one had to travel 8 kilometres from Sarajevo, and this road was strewn with barricades and obstacles. There were armed people on both sides within the circle and outside the circle. So there was total insecurity and uncertainty. In other words, it was not possible to travel normally and reach the Pretis factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, during the conflict, was the factory under the control of the ABiH or of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was fully under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, and according to the information that I have, around 700 people worked in that factory. That's the average annual figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the next part of the examination-in-chief concerns the Markale I incident, and I'm going to show you some videos and then a few photographs and my initial series of questions will be looking for fairly short response and then I'll give you an opportunity to explain the position in greater detail. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you participate in an investigation of the explosion which took place at Markale market on the 4th of February 1994?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I worked alongside three of my colleagues, but we were doing this investigation one day after the incident. I volunteered for this work, because I believed that the statements given on the previous day were not correct, and that it was, according to them, impossible to determine the origin of fire. So therefore I attempted, with my colleagues, to provide some additional information. The investigating judge who was on the spot authorised me and my colleagues to proceed with preparing this analysis, and we prepared this analysis in the next 36 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm going to play a video now and this video is P1711. This will be appearing on the screen in front of you. The first clip is from 6 minutes and 39 seconds and it will play until 7 minutes. If you could just look at this clip, Dr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You can stop it there, please. It stopped at 7 minutes and 13 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe just in a couple of sentences what you saw there, no need for detailed explanation at this stage.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this video, I can only see the effects of the fragments of a projectile on the ground, and I see that there was an attempt to establish the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the second clip is from 8 minutes and 32 seconds, and we'll play about 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We have stopped at 8 minutes and 46 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw in that clip?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can only assume this is most probably the point of impact of the projectile on the ground and that was an asphalt surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe in greater detail the surface at the Markale Market where the projectile impacted?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to tell you that based on this video or based on what I did?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Based on what you did.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived on the scene, I knew that an UNPROFOR soldier had dug out the tail-fin support from the ground. I went to this specific location to look at it. I asked for this tail-fin support to be brought to me. I looked at the opening where the stabiliser used to be. I tried to insert the support back into the hole that was there. I took out a few little stones that fell into it, and I inserted it without any effort. After that, I took the supports out again. I measured the depth of the penetration of the stabiliser. I made a sketch. And then, again, I returned the tail-fin support back to its place and, if I may say so, I tried to determine the descent angle or rather the angle of penetration by the tail-fin into the surface. So these were the basic measurements and activities that I performed, that served as the basis for some future analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In a sentence, could I ask you to describe the nature of the ground where the projectile impacted? How would you describe it, briefly?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a gravel surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe, is there a top surface followed by something underneath or what is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very simple: It was an asphalt surface. At the time when the blast and the impact took place, as a result of the detonation that affected this area, and the fragments, the asphalt was removed, there was a small funnel and there were lots of imprints or fragments in the wider area of the asphalt around the point of impact. Inside the soil, as a result of the penetration by the tail-fin, a canal was made, which was about 220 millimetres deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to show another clip now which is from 8 minutes and 54 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can stop it there, please. That was 9 minutes, we stopped at 9 minutes and 21 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe briefly what you saw in that clip?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What we see here is the front side of the tail-fin support protruding from the soil. Around it, you can see pieces of stone and probably pieces of asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We saw somebody digging in that clip. Was that the soldier to whom you referred in your earlier evidence?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. For my analysis, I used this particular video, on the basis of which I learned that this tail-fin support had penetrated the ground surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll go now to 19 minutes and 4 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who placed the chalk around the impact area?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did that, using chalk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we go now to 22 minutes and 9 seconds?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can stop there, please. Stopped at 22 minutes and 26 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain for the Court what the marking is that we see on the ground in that frame?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One arrow is pointing towards the north. The other arrow is pointing at the direction of the possible position where the mortar was, in other words, the direction from which the projectile came, based on some simple measurements, a 18-degree angle was established between north and east, and by using standard methodology, military methodology, the determination was made based on this asphalt surface which was very suitable for determining the direction and the origin of fire, and my estimate was that the probable origin of fire was 18 degrees plus/minus five degrees. I'm talking about the direction from which the projectile had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's 3.10, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 3.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My next couple of questions will focus on the measurement of the depth to which the projectile travelled in the ground before coming to rest. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up and, in fact, I'll just show you one final videoclip, in fact. This is from 22 minutes and 9 seconds, if we can play from there, please. Correction, 26 minutes and 50 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And we can stop it there. We stopped at 27 minutes and 28 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Before we get to the distance the projectile travelled before coming to rest, I just want to ask you a couple of questions based on what you saw in that clip. First of all, is what you saw in that clip consistent with detonation of the projectile upon contact with the ground or detonation upon contact with the roofing unit or a stall in the market?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a classical case of the impact of the projectile or contact with the ground, and the effects of the fuse activating --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no way that the projectile acted at a higher elevation or struck a roof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, if you could repeat your answer. The interpreters couldn't follow your answer in full.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we saw on the footage is a typical example of effects of the action of a high explosive projectile with -- upon contact with the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you, hypothetically speaking, no need for a long explanation, but if someone were to go up to the top of this building from where this video footage was taken and to throw off a 120-millimetre mortar projectile down to the ground, would that projectile detonate?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order for such a projectile to detonate, you would need to make an intervention on the fuse. The fuse would have to be armed, ready to act. Normally this happens only when the projectile leaves the barrel and is at a certain distance from the barrel of the weapon. In the event that somebody is that crazy or that brave and does carry out that intervention and does throw the projectile from the roof, they would need to make sure that the projectile doesn't rotate, but that it, upon contact, hits the head of the fuse, which nobody can guarantee. Besides that, it's also a question of whether that person at the point in time when they throw the projectile would themselves be exposed to the explosion; they could get wounded or killed. So it's an unrealistic scenario that we are talking about. You could only see that perhaps in some science fiction or action movies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now a photograph of the crater site. If we could call up P1970, and we will look briefly at two photographs, photograph 6, first of all, please. Now, if we could look at photograph 8, please. Mr. Zecevic, my question to you is this: Could you clarify whether in your measurement of the distance that the stabiliser had travelled before coming to rest, you were measuring from the top of the surface of the market or you were measuring from the top of what we see to be a depression in the surface caused by the explosion? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, at least I think I'm a professional. I measured from the ground level of the market, the asphalt surface of the ground, to the centre, and I measured in the centre of the crater a depth of 250 millimetres. If necessary, I could make a diagram in order to show how I went about the measurements, and I can also use one of the diagrams that I already have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's up to you to choose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've anticipated me very well. We have a diagram in one of your reports. This is the 2008 report which I won't be tendering, just solely to bring up a very useful diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up 10815 and could we go to page 41 in the B/C/S? There is no need to show the English. If we zoom in on the diagram which appears in the middle of this page. Perhaps we can zoom in on the one on the left, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does this assist you in explaining the distance that you measured and, if so, could you mark on the screen the distance to which the projectile travelled according to your measurements? Sorry, to which the stabiliser travelled before coming to rest.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you mark that with the letter A, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, while we have this diagram in front of me, I want to ask you a technical question about the reasons why sometimes a stabiliser embeds itself in the ground and sometimes a stabiliser is kicked back from the point of detonation. Could you describe, keeping in mind that we are all laypersons here, why the stabiliser sometimes goes into the ground and why sometimes it doesn't?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a characteristic of 120-millimetre mortar projectiles. There are three possible cases. The first case, which is indicated here as A, is when the projectile of a mortar comes at a pretty high velocity and hits the target, and then each element of that projectile has the same speed. At the point in time of the explosion there is a process of detonation that occurs. It's very brief. Which causes the fragmentation of the body of the projectile. If the speed of the -- of the rebounding of the stabiliser is less than the speed of the projectile, then the stabiliser will have enough energy to hit the surface and penetrate the ground. This is one of the indicators that we can use in order to assess the probable area of the launching of this projectile. Should I continue about these other two cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the second case, when the projectile is more or less equal to the rebound speed, and the 120-millimetre projectile, this speed can be about 170, plus or minus 20 metres, which can be calculated, then when the rebound speed is approximately the same, or equal to, the speed of the incoming projectile, and this is 170 metres, plus/minus 20 metres, then we will find the stabiliser close to the place of the explosion, and that then indicates to us the position from where the projectile was launched. The third case is when the speed of the incoming projectile is significantly lesser than the speed of the rebound of the stabiliser, and in that case, the stabiliser will be found scores of metres back in the direction from where the projectile came, and that will also give us an opportunity to make an assessment of the area from where the projectile was launched. I can say that these are God's laws, these are laws of mechanics, they don't depend on me or anyone else and this is something that can be plotted exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the Markale I incident, you said you created a report about that incident. Could I call up 10 -- sorry, could I ask you to sign this document and to put your name on it -- sorry, put today's date on it, I should say?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks] today is the 22nd; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. I'll tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we should be receiving on the screens in front of us the report which you created in respect of the Markale I incident, 10676. Perhaps if we can go to page 13 in B/C/S and page 8 in English, which contain a set of signatures, could you confirm who authored this report and what the report is?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is our analysis at the request of the investigating judge, and it's an analysis in which I took part. My colleagues Omerovic, Ahmed, Amir Kurtovic, and also Zijo Pekic, took part in the drafting of the analysis but he wasn't there when it was completed so he didn't sign it, because at the time he was in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on a couple of the conclusions you came to, which are summarised on this page of the report. I think we've dealt with conclusion number 5. You've already said that you measured the azimuth, or the direction from which the projectile came, to be 18 degrees, plus/minus 5 degrees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus on the conclusion number 7, the projectile's estimated angle of descent is 55 degrees to 65 degrees, the English translation contains in error in that regard. Who measured the estimated angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How did you measure it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I placed the stabiliser fins into the tunnel created by its penetration. I took an artillery square, which is a device that we use to determine the angle of a barrel of a weapon or some other element. I placed it at the front side of the stabiliser, and I set the angle of 60 degrees. Since it would be pretentious of me to say that the 60 degree angle was correct, because it's possible that there was some kind of motion during penetration, so some deviation, so I took that to be -- the value to be the range from 55 to 65 degrees, which any serious professional would also do in my case. So this angle is definitely correct, the range is correct, for that angle measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you replaced the stabiliser into the hole, could you describe whether it was quite a snug fit or loose fit? To what extent were you satisfied with the accuracy of replacing the stabiliser into the hole?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am 100 per cent sure that I positioned it in the way it should have been positioned, and there was no major deviation. For one reason. Later calculations that are accessible to everybody about the penetration into soft barriers indicate that the probable speed of penetration of the stabiliser was 60 plus/minus 20 metres per second. Perhaps this doesn't mean anything to you but 60 metres per second is 200 kilometres per hour. That would be the speed that the stabiliser fin penetrated the barrier. You know what happens when a car strikes a barrier at 200 kilometres per hour; it gets completely deformed. The car is destroyed. This stabiliser entered or penetrated through the barrier at exactly the same speed, or rather penetrated the surface, the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you distinguish, first of all, before we go any further, between the speed at which the stabiliser penetrated the ground and the speed at which the projectile itself was travelling at the moment of impact? Can you explain if there is a distinction there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If the speed of penetration is 60 metres plus/minus 20 per second, margin of error, and if the speed of the rebounding of the stabiliser is about 170 plus/minus 20 metres per second, later analysis that I carried out indicated that the minimum speed of the incoming projectile was 200 metres per second, the minimum speed, which automatically indicates that, in view of the impact speed, the launching zones would probably be five kilometres, 5.400 and 6.400 metres away from the place of the explosion. In any case, if we had found -- we would have found the stabiliser around the place of the explosion or back in the direction of the incoming angle. So this is a very clear thing for any mechanic, any mechanical engineer, this scenario is something that would be crystal clear for such a person. I did determine the zones, not the point of launch, but zones or areas from where the projectile could have possibly been launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe -- this is probably my last question before the break. Could you describe briefly how you came to the conclusion that the minimum speed of the incoming projectile was 200 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I tried to explain that earlier. If the rebound speed is -- actually, if the speed of penetration is 60 metres and the speed of rebound is plus or minus 20 metres, then the speed of the rebound of the stabiliser at the point of impact, at the time of the explosion would be 170, plus or minus 20 metres. So if we look at minimum values, you could have 40 metres here and you could have 50 metres here so that would be 190 metres per second. It could even be 240. I thought that most probably the speed would be 200 metres per second. So I'm talking about the speed of the incoming projectile, the speed of -- of penetration, and the speed of its rebound. So this is a calculation, and I thought that it was 200 metres, it could be 190 metres, 210, 220. I thought that it was at least 200 metres and that based on that, I could work out the possible area from where a projectile of this type was launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for half an hour, resume at 10 past 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think we are coming to the point where the Prosecutor was going to offer the Markale expert report into evidence and I just wanted to place on the record, outside of the presence of the witness, our objections to it. I know you've already ruled, but since we didn't have our objections on the record, I would just like to take a minute to do that. And our objections are that this witness is -- there is no showing that this witness is an expert in ballistics forensics, as opposed to the manufacture and design of ballistics. There's no showing he's ever done a crater analysis before this one, there is no showing that the -- the technique of replacing a stabiliser and making calculations from it is a legitimate one, and his work hasn't been peer-reviewed at all. And finally that he's not impartial, and in a few cases in the Sierra Leone Tribunal and in the ICTR, at least, they have disqualified persons who may otherwise have been considered to be expert, because of their lack of impartiality. And I'm referring specifically to a decision in the Charles Taylor case of the 19th of June, 2008, and one at the Akayesu case at the ICTR on the 9th of March, 1998. So for all of those reasons we have objected to the expert report being admitted as an expert report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours have already ruled, so I'll just place, I suppose, on the record the Prosecution's reasons for opposing the Defence's motion. This witness has been recognised as an expert in respect of the Markale I incident, both in the Galic case and in the Slobodan Milosevic case. He's also been recognised as an expert, generally speaking, in the Momcilo Perisic case and in the Dragomir Milosevic case. All of the issues raised by Mr. Robinson are appropriate areas for cross-examination. They don't disqualify the witness from acting as an expert, I think from the witness's -- I submit that from the witness's background, he is, in fact, one of the most qualified people coming out of the defence industry of the former Yugoslavia to comment on the impact of a 120-millimetre mortar projectile at a specific location in Sarajevo. There are very few people who are in fact more qualified than he is to make the observations that he's making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Yes, we agree with Mr. Gaynor in that the reasons referred to is not such that it should be disqualified as an expert. Very well, we'll bring in the witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to turn now to a page of your report relating to the Markale I incident and if we could look at page 7 in English and page 10 in B/C/S, on that page you give six possible distances for an angle of impact of 55 degrees and six possible distances for an angle of impact of 65 degrees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In fact, we can dispense with the English. I think the B/C/S is sufficient for this. First of all, could you tell us how much time you had to prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think around 36 hours. It was an extremely complicated situation. Everybody was excited and we were requested to finalise our report as soon as possible, and that was the best we could do at such a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the figures which appear in these two columns are in metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in the first column to the left, you indicate the range on charge 1, charge 2, charge 3, charge 4, charge 5 and charge 6, correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, based on the evidence you've given earlier today, do you exclude any of the potential distances which you set out in this report?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I exclude the possibility for the projectile to be launched with the first, second and third charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court why you exclude those possibilities?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Due to the fact because the launching speed of such projectiles -- actually those speeds were lower than the listed speed that the projectile should have had at the point of impact. Ballistics tells us that the speed at impact is never equal to the launching speed, so if I said that the minimum speed at impact was probably 200 metres per second, then the launching speed for the first charge would be 123 metres per second, for the second one 173, and for the third one 211 metres per second. In other words, the only possibility is that the fourth, fifth and sixth charges were used for launching the shell that hit Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I put the question -- a related question to you? If the stabiliser had not embedded itself in the ground to the extent that it had, what effect would that have had on your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That would probably include charge number 3, which is the range 4.120 to 3.622 metres from the point of explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your earlier evidence you said that the stabiliser embedded itself to an approximate distance of 250 millimetres in the ground. How relevant is that to excluding the possibility that the projectile had been fired from closer than 4.500 metres?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To put it simply, one can reach two conclusions. As for the second charge, or the third one, depending on the elevation from which the projectile was launched and I mean above sea level, with regard to point of explosion, we could find the stabiliser close to the place of explosion. So then we can speak about the distance ranging between 2.600 and 3.000 metres. From the moment when the stabiliser start penetrating the surface, one can speak about the possible zone with respect to a charge number 3. The deeper it went, if it reached 250 millimetres, we can say that that was -- it would be exclusively charges 4, 5 or 6. So if I may say, it is completely irrelevant whether it was 60, 50 or 70, 200, 250 or 150 millimetres depth. The only important point was whether stabiliser penetrated the ground or whether it was found in the vicinity of the point of explosion, or whether it was found discarded back to the direction of the launch. These are the only parameters that determine the potential launching zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the report at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, you've already ruled, so we don't have anything further, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The objection is noted. Yes, we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm going to turn now to the question of modified air-bombs. Could we call up 65 ter 08347, please? Now, for the benefit of the court, if you intend to consult anything other than your copy of the modified air-bomb, please inform the Court. Do you understand that? Your copy of the modified air-bomb report, I should say. Very well. Now, first of all, the document on the screen in front of you, could you confirm what that is?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an analysis that I made for the Prosecution in the General Milosevic case. It applies to the use of modified aircraft bombs during the siege of Sarajevo in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could -- I'll be asking some questions about this but I'd like to tender it at this stage, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P2318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we turn now to page 68 of the report in B/C/S, page 74 in English? My first set of questions will focus on the factors affecting the accuracy and the precision of modified air-bombs. Those are not in fact the pages I was looking for. If you give me a moment, please. If we could go to page 76 in B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 82 in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The page I want it is paginated differently to the e-court version. So perhaps if we could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there a probability, you're referring to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, this is the page I want, right in front of us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could just focus in really on the diagram of that projectile there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need English page as well. Page 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you just briefly confirm that this is a diagram which you made of a modified FAB 250?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a diagram of the modified rocket assisted bomb, FAB 250. It contains three rocket engines, a stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The diagram was drawn based on the fragments retrieved in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we can keep this page on the screen. Elsewhere in your report, you describe some of the factors affecting the accuracy and precision of modified air-bombs. One of the -- this is at page 87 of your report in English and page 79 in B/C/S. One of the first factors you describe is that they did not have complex assemblies for controlling individual phases of the bomb's action. I want you to focus on the ignition phase. Could you describe for the Court what effect it would have on the flight of the projectile if one of the three rockets were to be ignited ever so slightly later than the other two?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Each of these systems was equipped with three independent rocket engines. They were supposed to activate simultaneously. Based on the documents available to me, the assembling of the rocket system was carried out by using predominantly 122 Grad rocket engines, or 128 Organj engines or 127 engines of K-15 guided missiles. The most important problem is that all these engines act independently of each other, which can produce a consequence that each of them would have the difference in the pressure of burning, which means the force would be different during the flight, and this will subsequently cause the deviation from the direction of the rocket that had been previously anticipated, and of course it will miss the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is this the same as another factor which you've mentioned in your report where you said that these modified projectiles did not have a means of equalising combustion pressure in the rocket motor? Is that a separate issue or is that the issue that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. In the first system that I found in January of 1994, the rocket engines were interconnected in order to equalise the combustion pressure which would compensate for some of the difference between the pressures within each of these engines. These engines consisting of three pieces, did not have pressure compensators, which cause the increased dispersion at the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, elsewhere in your report you said that the centring of the axes in the rocket motors, in the rocket structure, was unsatisfactory. Could you explain briefly to the Court what effect a slightly non-parallel fixing of the rocket motors would have on the accuracy and precision of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This three-rocket engine system is an extremely primitive version of a rocket system. Far better technologically would be the system with four engines that were in use in the beginning of January 1994. This other system was made without using the potential that the Pretis company had. It was below or substandard manufacture. As a result, it could cause, at any point in time, for any of these systems not to have equal performance rates, and the possibility of hitting a planned target was extremely low.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain - actually just staying on that point - a slightly non-parallel alignment of the rocket motors, could you focus very much on that issue, how would that affect the flight of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It would cause lateral deviation from the direction. So it's a complex question. At any rate, this will cause a lateral disturbance which would cause the projectile to turn left, right, upwards or downwards, depending on when and how this system was assembled. It was not only rocket engines that were key elements to the system. The stabilising system used here was equally extremely negatively designed, from the point of view of flight stability, and it caused additional dispersion at the targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is meant by circular error probability, sometimes referred to as CEP in English?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was a statistical parameter which indicates the zone or, rather, the radius which says that of the 120 projectiles, 50 would fall in a zone. If we look at, for example, 155-millimetre shell, the CEP at the distance of 24 kilometres would be 360 metres in diameter. That would be the circle within which, of the 150 projectiles, 50 would fall in that zone and the remaining would fall out of that zone. It has been quite clearly stated that non-guided rocket or artillery weapon can -- can target multiple targets. It could only target, for example, a football playground. So there is not a single rocket system or artillery system that can hit a house from a distance of 8 to 10 kilometres. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. Perhaps it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 4.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Before the break you described what circular error probability is. Would you be able to give the Court an estimate of the circular error probability of the modified FAB air-bombs which were used on Sarajevo during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that on the basis of the analysis that I tried to provide here with my associates, that the surface where those projectiles would fall would be from 60 to 250 metres, the surface. That would be the circular error probability. You could probably derive it from that to be some 250 metres in radius.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: During your period at Pretis, you worked on the development of new weapon systems; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: About how long would weapons system be in the testing and development phase before it was ready to be used?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Usually a new serious system would take five to seven years to develop. Often it would be ten years. After one or two years, you would quickly define the basic concept and then the rest of the time would be spent to bring the system up to the situation where you could predict its performance. So it would take a minimum of five to seven years for this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you compare, on the one hand, the weapon systems developed in Pretis before the conflict and, on the other, the modified air-bombs which were used on Sarajevo during the conflict, and offer the Court your observations as to the accuracy of the modified air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The process of developing a new system is extremely complex, and demands the participation of a number of organisational systems. If Pretis thus was supposed to develop a new system, it had to include people who would be working on design, people who would be working on the manufacture of components, people who would be working on the inspection of the production process, and also they had to engage technical testing centres that were within the JNA system. This required complete equipment to measure velocity, range, the behaviour of the projectile in flight. You had to include rocket fuel production facilities, explosives production facilities, you had to include people who were working on the firing tables. This would probably be done by the military technical institute from Belgrade in most cases. And only then, after four to five years, the factory would be in a position to say that it had completely mastered the development of a new system and its manufacture and then you would proceed to the production of the zero series, which would then be given to the technical testing centre, which, independently of the factory, would test the weapon independent of the factory that produced that particular system. And then that centre would submit the final suggestions as to whether that system would be part of the weapon systems or not. This is an extremely complex process requiring the engagement of a large number of people, large amount of funds, equipment, and a large amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And briefly "yes" or "no", on the basis of what you were able to establish in your preparation of this report, did the modified air-bomb system go through anything like that process? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the basis of your expert analysis of the modified air-bomb and of your own experience, are you able to offer an opinion as to whether the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had modified air-bomb systems during the war?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That is, it did not have such systems, correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have the technical capacity to produce such systems. They didn't have the material resources. They didn't have the production plants. And they didn't have the power potential or capability in order to manufacture these devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the concept of fuel air, as opposed to TNT, in respect of the content of the air-bombs. Can you tell the Court briefly which has more destructive capacity, a bomb filled with TNT or one filled with a fuel-air mix?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The question is not precise, but I can try to give you an answer as to why the question is not precise. I can answer the question, but I can also explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A warhead with a hard explosive such as TNT, at the moment it hits the target and when the fuse is activated, which reacts within an interval of 200 to 300 millionth parts of a second, activates the detonation, the hard explosive begins to turn into gaseous detonation products, and very soon the metal body of the projectile, because of extremely high pressure within the projectile, which is measured in 2 to 300.000 bars and the temperature of 3 to 4.000 degrees Centigrade begins to expand, meaning the metal body, under the effect of such high pressure, grows to four or five times the volume and that's when the fragmentation begins. When the fragmentation begins, the detonation products leave the body of the projectile creating an extremely high pressure impulse, a very high value, which radically, quickly, decreases upon impact. The entire fragmentation process lasts some 50, 60 or 70 millionth parts of a second. With aerosol bombs, or projectiles, the process is completely different. First, the body of such a projectile has to be shattered with a hard explosive, which causes the fuel explosive to mix with the air around it. It evaporates and expands within a couple of parts of a second, within -- or a couple of second, it mixes with the surrounding air, of the aerosol, with the neighbouring air, and then you need an outside initiation, an outside source of energy, these are usually explosive charges, two or three explosive charges, which then initiate the process of detonation of the aerosol explosive. In the meantime the aerosol has expanded over a wider area, some 10, 20 or 30 metres broad, and then there is the activation, but the pressure in this process now is 20 to 30 bars, not hundreds or thousands of bars, and the time required for this pressure process with the aerosol bomb is much longer, and the aerosol bomb has a very good destructive effect on buildings, which are tagged as soft targets, people, bunkers, some warehousing facilities, airplanes, different depots and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If I can ask you this: You said in your report that the fuel-air system was originally developed to clear vegetation in Vietnam; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. So that choppers could land.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you comment on whether -- which system, the TNT system or the fuel-air system, would be more appropriate for the destruction of buildings and which would be more appropriate for destruction of people?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a complex question. If human targets in the open are involved, then there is a greater probability, when a TNT projectile impacts a zone with human targets, that, not the effect of pressure, but the fragmentation effect will cause the destruction of human targets. But if the human targets are dug in in bunkers or if they are dug in, as in the case of Vietnam, in subterranean tunnels, then the air-bomb system is extremely effective. In the same way, if the target is a housing facility, a building, then a greater effect for internal structures and human targets would be caused by the aerosol system, but in order to achieve that, you would really need to be a very talented person in order to be able to strike at urban parts of towns with air-bombs. This is not something that is present in any doctrine of any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your report, you've commented on a number of specific incidents concerning the use of modified air-bombs in Sarajevo in 1995. And in most of those cases, you consider, according to your report, that the air-bombs in question contained fuel-air rather than TNT. Could you identify for the Court, in brief terms, what are the factors that you took into account in determining whether the projectile contained a fuel-air mix or TNT?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the event that the system had a hard-type explosive such as TNT, at the moment of impact on the target, the air-bomb which can weigh as much as 220 kilograms and contains over 90 kilograms of hard explosives would generate an extremely high blast effect, i.e. pressure, and a large number of fragments, which would have as a consequence that the rocket engines and the stabilisers would be ejected very far from the point of impact. In the case of all the systems that I analysed in the Sarajevo area in my analysis, I always found rocket engines or parts of rocket engines at the point of impact with the stabiliser fins. This is a fact that is not possible to dispute. This is identical, as in the 120-millimetre mortar projectiles. But in the case of the 120-millimetre mortar shell, you have 2.2 kilograms of TNT and in the air-bombs you have 90 kilograms of TNT. This is the comparison between the two projectiles, the mortar projectile and the air-bomb. These are the main reasons; there are other reasons but they are not as crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My question was specifically how you could tell that it was an air-bomb filled with a fuel-air mix compared to an air-bomb filled with TNT. Does that -- do you have any further observations to make?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's very simple. In case that a TNT air-bomb explodes near a building, the air-bomb with TNT generates over 7.000 fragments, more than 7 milligrams of mass -- 7 grams of mass. So any neighbouring area would be absolutely perforated by lots and lots of fragments. I did not have the opportunity to see that, in any case. If a TNT air-bomb hit a house or a building, and if the explosion occurred within a house, of 90 kilograms of TNT, all the walls would be blasted towards the outside. In some cases, I showed clearly that this was not the case, that in the middle of the blast area, there would be a wall still standing straight because the aerosol acted with equal force on either side of the wall and prevented that wall from crumbling; this is in Hrasnica. So all the analysis that were carried out indicate that an aerosol system was used, in each one of those cases, as in the examples in the report that you are showing to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge and on the basis of your inspection at the sites you describe in your report, did the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have the technical capacity to produce aerosol bombs during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you like a descriptive answer or a short answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd prefer a short answer, please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honours require further analysis. I'll keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That ends this portion of your examination-in-chief. I now want to show you a few documents that you've had a chance to review earlier. Can I call up 15842, please? A couple of these documents are delivery documents concerning munitions and I think it's fair to say that they are quite difficult to follow for --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do have an intervention. Here it says 7 milligrams, but actually it's a mass of seven grams. This is a vast difference so 7.000 fragments of 5 grams mass or more. 5 grams mass or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you for that. If we could turn to the next page of the document on the screen, please? I can provide a hard copy for you if it's more comfortable. Could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] It would help if he learned what is the origin and who made those marks by pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, if there are any annotations, Mr. Zecevic, made by pen, you can ignore those, they are simply marks which happen to be on my copy, but I'll get him to explain what the document is, if that allays Mr. Karadzic's concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the document, witness, please, and first of all just tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch list of air-bombs weighing 250 kilograms, of the 5th of April 1995, speaking that as of the 1st of January 1994 until the 31st of December 1994, the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, the Main Staff in Pale, dispatched 95 bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is there anything else in that document concerning air-bombs that you wish to comment on?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It states FAB 250 here. So these are air-bombs, FAB 250. There is the price of that bomb, but I don't know in which currency it's presented.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist? The Main Staff was never in Pale. Does the Prosecutor, Mr. Gaynor, have another witness to clarify the origin of this document because there was never a Main Staff in Pale. The Main Staff was some 50 kilometres away from Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it is a proper subject for you to explore during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not directed at the witness, but at Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what I said is your intervention is not helpful at this moment, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you just confirm, you said it's a dispatch list. Could you tell who it's from and who it's to?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really say because you cannot see who this is sending -- who is sending this ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. On the basis of the witness's identification of the munitions, I'll tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, given some question as to its authenticity, that we would be objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the witness was not able to -- I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we are not satisfied as to its foundation or authenticity, we will not admit this at this stage, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll move on to the next document, which is 15709. Dr. Zecevic, you can put down that document. A document will appear on your screen in a moment. Could you tell us what this document appears to be?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a report about the ammunition issued from the holding Pretis further to orders of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, sent by the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, the logistics sector, on the 5th of December, 1993, sent to the Main Staff -- to the Defence Ministry of Republika Srpska, stating that in the period from the 1st of January 1993 to the 30th of November 1993, the following resources have been issued from the holding company Pretis, further to orders by the VRS Main Staff. And then we have the order number, the type of ammunition, the quantity of the ammunition, and the military unit to which the -- this ammunition was supplied to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In this document in a number of locations we see mortar 120-millimetre MB. Would you be able to comment on what that is?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 82-millimetre mine, MB, mortar shell, and a mortar shell of 120 millimetres. You have that. You have 100, 120, pieces. Then you have 82-millimetre mortar shells, 600 pieces. Then up 120-millimetre mortar shell, 300 pieces. Then 120 millimetre, 500 pieces. Then you have some 500 contact-fuse bullets. This is what I can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are these references to 120 millimetre mortars, is that the same kind of projectile that impacted at Markale Market?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in a number of the projectiles which the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, I've forgotten that we should have taken a break. We will take a break for five minutes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. --- Break taken at 5.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has received information about markings on 120-millimetre projectiles containing the letters KB, Cyrillic letters, KB, which in Latin is KV. Do you happen to know what those mean?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the code name for the ammunition factory called Krusik Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does that suggest that such parts were made in the Krusik factory in Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not a single element of the ammunition in the former Yugoslavia could leave the factory without marking being stamped by the factory, the code name of the factory, which is also in line with international regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the document you've just looked at, there is a reference to quite significant quantities of 120-illimetre mortars being issued from Pretis, correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. It just said that this ammunition was delivered from Pretis to Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Vogosca Brigade, and so on and so forth. So probably the ammunition was delivered from that particular factory because there is no other ammunition factory in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on the basis of your experience prior to the conflict, the relationship between Pretis in Vogosca and Krusik in Valjevo in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, Krusik Valjevo was a factory producing guided rocket missile systems and 60-, 82- and 120-millimetre mortar shells. It also manufactured base charge for mortar shells. Pretis, if they produced 120-millimetre shell, would purchase base charge from Krusik as one of the components that they required. Pretis produced non-guided systems, anti-tank projectiles and aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the document the witness commented on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We object, Mr. President. We don't think this is a proper witness to tender this type of document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You do not challenge the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
