utterances.text: We don't really know the authenticity of the document, but I note that it has a seal and a signature on the last page, but Dr. Karadzic has never seen this before, so he's not in a position to stipulate to its authenticity. But in any event, this is -- the kind of comments that this witness has made about the document, when you admit a document for all purposes, it seems like that's a little extreme to admit this document based on the kind of comments that he's made on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, do you like to reply to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to ask the question -- the witness further questions. He did work at Pretis for 17 years. He is intimately familiar with documentation relating to the production by Pretis of ammunition. He's confirmed that this -- he confirmed that this document refers to the delivery of 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre mortar projectiles to the Vogosca Brigade, the Rajlovac Brigade, the SRKs. He's confirmed essentially what this document is. Now, we can ask him questions about the person who signed the document, if you wish, in a further effort to establish its authenticity. I have to say I'm somewhat surprised that the Defence is objecting at this stage to the document. They haven't objected to many VRS documents in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think our problem with this is that this witness, by December 5th, 1993, when this document was authored was no longer in any way connected with the VRS, the Pretis or any of this information, so he's commenting on something that really he can't speak to, other than in very general way, and so we don't think that that is sufficient to make a document admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is satisfied with the authenticity of the document, and given that the witness was able to give some context to this document, we will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Mr. President. Could I have 07720, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, witness, could you comment on the heading and general appearance of this document? Does it -- where does it appear to have been issued from?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a standard document, or better to say an official document issued by Pretis factory which was part of UNIS group so you have the logo of UNIS and Pretis, and it says, "Pretis Sarajevo". Pretis is an abbreviation of the enterprise Tito Sarajevo. We have the address, 71-320 Vogosca, that was the pre-war address. Then Igman Mars Street number 24, telephone 071, area code number for Sarajevo. So this is a typical letterhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you comment on the signature and stamp of this document?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about the signature, but I can tell you that Milorad Motika, an engineer, was a colleague of mine before the war. I knew him and we were on relatively good terms. This stamp was not the one used before the war. It's a more recent one because it says, "Pretis holding Vogosca enterprise." There is no UNIS logo. But it says UNIS, Pretis holding enterprise Vogosca. I cannot say this with 100 per cent certainty, because transformation took place immediately before the war, which was conducive to the change of the stamp, but as I said, I know the director of Pretis holding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to know when Milorad Motika was appointed as director of Pretis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After the war began.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have recorded in the transcript that this witness said that Motika was an industrious man? Can he confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document refers to -- I'll read out the words in the English language: "660 FAB 250 aerial bombs without stabilisers with fuses, so we can complete the 122-millimetre rocket engines." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you able to explain what the word "complete" means in this context?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this context, as I understand it based on my experience, means that it was necessary to secure FAB 250 bombs with fuses and to deliver 122-millimetre rocket engines. Now, Pretis would manufacture additional parts in order to complete these systems, which is the connection between the engines and the aerial bomb, the stabiliser systems, et cetera, because at the end it says, "All other parts for rocket bombs."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 15754, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you able to see that, Dr. Zecevic? I have a clean, hard copy here if you wish me to provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If it's no trouble. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you able to describe what that document is?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the VRS, logistics sector, 14th, I think June, 1995, delivers to the command of the 27th Logistics Brigade and the commander of the 35th Logistics Brigade, and to Pretis, for information only, reference official document strictly confidential, from 1995, it is a -- requested that the 27th Logistics Brigade -- I'm sorry, take over from the 35th Logistics Brigade and hand over to Pretis, 30 pieces and 20.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please read slowly all the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bombs will be taken over -- upon takeover, the bombs, along with the corresponding number of 128-millimetre rocket engines - 110 pieces, shall be transported and handed over at holding Pretis or to holding Pretis for assembling. This is not what is written in this document. Number 2, complete the bombs in the following manner. Ten FAB 100, which are 100 kilogram aerial bombs with three motors each; 20 FAB 100 with one engine each and immediately they made a correction by hand and said, 30 pieces with one engine and finally 20 pieces, FAB 250, with three engines each. Upon completing the aerial bombs shall be taken over and stored by the 27th Logistics Base. Commence the implementation of this task immediately, and upon completion the command of the 27th logistics Base Shall inform this staff accordingly. By authorisation of the chief Lieutenant-Colonel Miroslav Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the reference in this document to FAB 100 with three motors each, briefly tell us what you believe that to be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is probably relating to completing these rocket systems with aerosol explosives. That's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now we see reference to FAB 100s with three motors and FAB 100s with one motor.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the more typical delivery system for the FAB 100?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: FAB 100 used only one rocket engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the FAB 250?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Normally three or four. More likely it would be three, because the majority of the remnants found indicate that there were three rocket engines, although there are reports that there were four rocket engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At the end of the first paragraph, there is a reference to, "These bombs are to be transported and handed over to HD Pretis for assembling." Briefly tell us what the word "assembling" means, on the basis of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of aerial bombs was for them to be dropped from aircraft. In this instance, the connection between aerial bomb and rocket engine meant that a new rocket system would be made consisting of FAB 250 warhead and three 128-millimetre rocket engines. In other words, that would be similar to the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Projectiles that targeted Sarajevo back in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the same reason, we will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, it's time to take another break. Gain very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will break for half an hour this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to note for the record before we go on that the document which was not admitted earlier, 65 ter 15842, the Prosecution's internal records state that that was seized from the premises of the Pretis factory in Vogosca following the reintegration of Sarajevo. I'll continue with the examination-in-chief. Could I call up 65 ter 13542, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you have a brief read of that document, witness. There is no need to read it out verbatim, we have the translation, but just tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is about the forming of an executive team on the basis of a decision by the President of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, that would include a number of people whose task would be to equip the armed forces, in terms of materiel and equipment, and to transfer the relevant means from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and place them in agreed-upon locations and it asks that the report on the executed assignment be sent to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You see a number of names on that document. Do you happen to know any of those people yourself?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know Branko Prodanovic, and I also had the opportunity to see Momcilo Mandic on television. It's also possible that I know Spasoje Orasanin as well, Colonel Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did any of those individuals work at Pretis before the war or did any of them work at Pretis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Branko Prodanovic worked in Pretis for many years. He's an economist by profession. And just before the war, he was the director-general of Pretis. According to my information, a couple of months after the war began, he left that position and became the representative of the Pretis company in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We object to this. First on relevance. It doesn't relate to air-bombs that we could tell or anything manufactured by Pretis that we could tell from the face of it. And secondly I don't think the witness has spoken enough to the document other than to identify an individual. If that becomes the test then it will really expand the Chamber's guidelines to beyond something that is reasonable, if simply knowing an individual is enough to get a document admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can respond. I note that there is no objection to the authenticity of it so far. In his evidence, the witness has referred to cooperation between locations in the FRY and in the Bosnian Serb-held part of Bosnia during the conflict, in relation to the supply of parts from Krusik Valjevo, specifically to Pretis, and the assembly of, specifically, modified air-bombs at Pretis, as well as the relationship between stabilisers produced at Krusik Valjevo and the issuance of ammunition from Pretis. So he has testified about cooperation between authorities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in the Republika Srpska during the relevant period and he's identified a person who worked at Pretis on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless the Defence is not challenging the authenticity, we find it relevant and of probative value. On that basis we will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions. I do have one point which relates to the oral submissions made by Mr. Robinson earlier. We can make it in the absence of the witness or I can simply note it at this stage, as Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll hear about it in the next break, after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. As I indicated, Dr. Zecevic, you will be asked -- cross-examined by Mr. Karadzic. So are you ready to start, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Good evening to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would first like to dwell on your views and your findings in relation to the modified air-bombs. Would you agree that the main difference between the aerosol bombs and bombs with classic explosive charges, such as TNT, are as follows: The aerosol bomb creates a considerably less pressure compared to bombs with classic explosive charges, but that pressure lasts much longer? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you will be aware of this but given that Mr. Karadzic and you are speaking the same language, it's important to put a pause between the question and answer so that the interpreters can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You established that, you've said that that was correct, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For a classic explosion, it is not necessary to have oxygen from the air?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What is a classic explosive for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: TNT is a classic explosive.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. It doesn't need oxygen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And explosives that are used in aerosol bombs need to mix with air; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that have an effect on the construction of each type of bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us briefly what the difference would be in the construction?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A classic air-bomb consists of the body, the front and rear fuse, stabiliser, and often it has a braking device. Hard explosive TNT or a mixture of TNT and aluminium is placed inside the body. With the aerosol bomb, there is a primer -- primary explosive charge for which hard explosives are used. And then secondary explosive charges and there is also a liquid that is placed in the body of the bomb. At the point of impact, the primary explosive charge destroys the body of the air-bomb, the gas or the liquid is released, it evaporates, mixes with the air, and then the secondary fuses, after a certain amount of time, are ejected into the area around the place of the explosion and they activate the explosive mixture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for being so concise. Would we agree that the bomb with the classic explosive acts on a smaller area and that is why it can create craters?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the blast wave effect only, or do you mean the overall effect of the air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The overall effect of the air-bomb.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: An air-bomb with TNT creates a destructive effect in the blast zone. It destroys things in the area. And the fragments created in the detonation can damage people and objects within a radius of several hundred metres around the immediate explosion area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it leaves a crater, does it not?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Depending on whether the fuse is a contact fuse, a close -- immediate contact fuse or a delayed fuse. In any case, if it's a contact fuse, there would be a crater. In case there is a delayed fuse effect the crater will be larger, or it will not be there at all depending on the period of delay because this can be detonated within a building or a bunker. If it's a contact fuse, the effect primarily is of fragmentation which includes -- which increases the kill zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would we agree that the aerosol explosives act on a larger area and do not create a crater?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If a contact fuse is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do we agree that with classic explosives, a human being behind a shield can survive, if there is some kind of barrier between the person and the explosive?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that this barrier does not provide protection in the case of an air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the distance where that person is from the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If they are at the same distance, let's say, of 10 to 15 metres in each case, the barrier can protect against classic explosive and the aerosol bomb will not be able to provide the protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your answer was?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Dr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course, I apologise. In the event that the mixing proceeds very well, of the liquid aerosol with the air, at the same distance of 10 to 15 metres from the centre of the explosion, the person would not manage to get through it unharmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meaning that the person would not be able to survive?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a complex question, depending on the amount of the explosive effect at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am just trying to simplify this double negation. Would not manage to get through it unharmed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the person would be wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 26th and the 27th of February -- "to say the least" was not recorded in the transcript, "to say the least" is not in the transcript. So the least consequence would be wounding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 26th and the 27th of February, you said, as far as the air bombs are concerned, this is something that I made conclusions on by myself. The reasons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused is kindly asked to tell the interpreters where he's reading from and to read slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters were not able to follow you. They wanted to know where you are reading from but slow down when you're reading something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm just rushing because of time. For this witness we really need a lot of time but I do also take into account his situation. Yes, can we look into e-court 65 ter 09997? Page 4 in the Serbian version, and page 4 in the English version also. Paragraph 6 in the Serbian version and paragraph 6 in the English version. So it's identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this part regarding the air-bombs? Regarding the air-bombs in English. Let me repeat that: "Regarding the air bombs, I came to my own conclusions. It is clear to me that the explosions were caused by air-fuel explosions. The same type of weapons were used by the USA in Vietnam, by the Russians in Afghanistan, and by the Israelis in the Middle East. These projectiles have a blast effect where modified aircraft bombs also cause a fragmentation effect?" Was that your position?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please remind me to whom I gave this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe you provided the statement to the OTP. Can we look at page 1. This is page 4. Let's look at page 1 so that Mr. Zecevic can identify the document.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we now go back to page 4 now, please? Mr. Zecevic, does this mean that liquid explosives behave in the same way as fuel? They can have fuel combustion or flame combustion or they can be combustible by an explosion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. This is a mistake. Fuel bombs are a fuel-air explosive. They have nothing to do with aeroplane fuel. It's a fuel bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please tell us what is the original and what is the translation here?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just provide a comment here, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During all of my testimonies, for the OTP, whenever I gave a statement, the statement was first written in the English. Later it was translated back to one of our languages, depending on the ability of the interpreter, the terminology -- their grasp of terminology, they would make these statements. All my objections, in the sense that this term does not correspond to this particular term, they would believe that that was not so important, those objections of mine. So I'm going to say this: This is not aeroplane fuel that we are talking about. The problem here is of a purely linguistic nature. I still stand by what I said, that we are talking about aerosol explosives in English, aerosol weapons have a fuel-air weapon, that is their description but somebody might describe that as aircraft fuel. Fuel-air fire, fuel-air weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What it says here is air-fuel, in English air-fuel explosion. And in the original it says, "avionsko gorivo," so the Serbian version is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there is an error in the sense of the terminology that is being used. This is a question of The Hague Tribunal and the prosecutor's office. It's a question of the kind of interpreters and the kind of investigators that they hire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have for the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have the last break for today, five minutes. --- Break taken at 6.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought you wanted to make your observation but we'll hear from you later on, then. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, can I direct your attention in this same document to paragraph 7, which is the next one, and line 3, but before that, I would like the record to show that the witness has said that both versions, the English and the Serbian ones, were wrong.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not wrong but imprecise in linguistic terms, and I think that's a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that at Zuc, at Zuc hill, you had a first encounter with aerial bomb, and you were taken there by a friend of yours who showed you the remnants of that new weapon?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't go to Zuc, but, rather, these remnants were brought close to my house where the staff of that unit was headquartered and I was invited to come over and look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which unit are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was close to your house?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: About 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please look at this document. It reads here -- the transcript does not show that you said that the staff was close to your house. Correction, not what, but, rather, staff was close to your house. Let me read you what it says here: "He showed me the remnants of a rocket engines that propelled them. It was a 3 and a half metres long pipe, 500 millimetres in diameter, that was retrieved on the spot. The warhead, however, was not located. After an analysis of the rear part of the projectile, I noticed that this was not an improvised device but rather a highly professional one. I could tell this from the quality of finish. The projectile had four Russian rocket engines of 120-millimetre M21 Grad type and in the middle a container with a parachute." Is this what you stated on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking. My report, which is very precise, is held by the OTP, and you can see the exact report with exact terminology. Now, I'm repeating this once again, that the methodology of how witnesses are interviewed, the terminology that I used and the terminology that the people who interpreted me used and compiled the statements, did not correspond fully to what I say, but the essence remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, then let's look at that report of yours. That's 65 ter 08347. 65 ter 08347. Let's first look at page 1. Can we have the English version as well? Is this the report that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. This is a report from February 1994. And it is an integral part of this report. It's at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see what you said in this report and to that end can we see page 6 in Serbian? And I think it's the same page in English. Now, if this is page 6, is this page 6? It says page 2 here. Number 6 in the Serbian, and we'll see which page it corresponds in the English version. Maybe one page back in e-court. We need paragraph 2 - let's see - paragraph 2, line 5. That's page 6 in e-court. Yes, now it's all right. Page 2 in the report and number 6 in e-court. Let us now look at it. Somewhere in the middle of the paragraph, this is a -- line 5 from the top, in paragraph 2. "I examined the fragments of the projectile which consisted of a system comprising four rocket motors of 122-millimetre Grad type and the fifth container for a parachute system. The rocket's motors were connected together at the front with the system for equalising combustion pressure in the chambers and they were fitted in an aluminium plate. These helped to centre the rocket motors and facilitated the link with the warhead section of the rocket projectile."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see on the screen what you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We need the next page in the Serbian version so look at paragraph 2, line 5, which begins, "I have examined."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In English, we have it in English. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "On the section towards the nozzles of the rocket motors, there was a stabilising section of the projectile which encompassed the motor assembly. Colour of the rocket motors and the markings on the nozzles fully correspond to Russian military standards." Is this what is written here?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how come that you are not describing any longer this pipe of 500 millimetres in diameter and 3 to 5 metres long?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This 500 millimetre pipe was misinterpreted. That should have been a warhead with 500-millimetre diametre, and the support which connected the war head with the rocket propellant had 500 millimetres in diameter. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they didn't find the warhead?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It makes sense because the warhead had exploded. That's why they brought the fragments to me to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, here we have the mention of the pressure equalising system which you don't mention in your previous statement.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is a precise technical report that I provided, whereas what you're talking about was the statement that I was asked by an investigator to give sometime in February 1996. In other words, the technical report that I compiled and signed as an expert is meritorious, and it reflects my technical observations. What essentially, with the exception of terminological explanation of certain issues, it is completely identical to what is contained in the statement given to the OTP. There is no contradictory statement. My statements, part of my statements, were probably misinterpreted but it doesn't change the style or the essence of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that we should rather stick to your report than your statement?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer to that. I maintain that basically neither of these things exclude one another. There are only erroneous linguistic interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your reports, you claimed that Sarajevo was targeted by aerosol bombs. Were those bombs similar to the one that was brought to you from Zuc?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of aerosol bombs were used to target Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a simpler version of an aerosol system compared to the one that was located at Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll try to make this more precise. You claimed that Sarajevo was being targeted by two types of bombs, FAB 100 and FAB 250; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not only claim that. I attached photographs of an unexploded FAB 100 millimetre bomb and I gave them to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which one of those is aerosol?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: FAB 250.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what does this acronym FAB stand for?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Russian, it's general purpose bomb, if translated into English, or in Russian, a bomb that produces a blast effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you still believe that this was an aerosol bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's not what I think; I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. What is contact fuse? Is that a fuse?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Fuse is -- contact fuse is, when you have unexploded devices on a pile and you activate them, and you create a contact-fuse detonation whose primary purpose is to cause devastation and destruction and not its primary role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your report, and we might call it up, it's 0037 -- 3282, 1D3282. While we are waiting, can you tell me, according to what you knew, where were aerosol bombs manufactured?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to aerosol bombs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The development of aerosol bombs was initiated at Pretis before the war. Sometime in 1987, the first phase of development was completed. After 1988, Colonel Vladan Tomic moved to Belgrade, he had been the project manager, and he took with him the whole set of documents relating to the development of aerosol bombs. According to what I know, because I personally saw these aerosol bombs, two or three months ago, because the UNDP agency appointed me to be the person who would recommend how to destroy 24 unexploded aerosol bombs kept in BH storages, and 34 rocket-assisted bombs that had been produced by Krusik in 1994, so as I said, I personally saw these bombs as well as the rocket-assisted bombs with four rocket engines that are currently kept in the depot of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 21 of this document? You say here that they were produced in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think that the terms you're using are not accurate. I gave you my interpretation relating to aerosol bombs. However, if you're asking me about rocket-assisted aerosol bombs, then I can give you a different answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Rocket-assisted aerosol bombs were assembled completely and mechanically at Pretis. This is where the connection of the aerosol bomb body was made, the connecting parts were made to connect rocket engines, also produced were stabilisers and all these parts were, after that, delivered to one of the logistics bases of the Main Staff of the VRS, where the -- these were charged, where aerosol explosive is something I can't tell you because I don't have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were aerosol bombs manufactured?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Aerosol bombs in general, or are you talking about a specific period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The aerosol bombs that you claim were fired at Sarajevo, where were they manufactured?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said that rocket-assisted aerosol bombs were used to target Sarajevo. In order to use aerosol bombs, one would need to use aircraft to drop them. If you say, and if you're asking me, about rocket-assisted aerosol bombs, one version of them was manufactured or, rather, assembled at Pretis, because air-bombs, FAB 250, had been manufactured before the war and delivered to the JNA. It can be seen from documents that these air-bombs and rocket engines, 122 or 128, were shipped back to Pretis where an assembly of an improvised rocket system was carried out, which consisted of potentially aerosol explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we still didn't get an answer from you, where this aerosol segment of the bomb was manufactured. I'm not talking about the propelling section. Where the aerosol bomb was manufactured.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I am reiterating my clear and precise answer: The full assembling of the rocket-assisted system that was made up of an air-bomb, FAB 250, a connection to the rocket engine, and stabiliser, was something that was done at Pretis. The charging of the air-bomb was not done in Pretis because in my opinion, and based on my experience, only the military technical institute from Belgrade could have done that or the people from the Vinca nuclear institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, you don't know where they were produced. You suppose that it was somewhere in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you want me to tell you the whole story again and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you acquire information that Pretis delivered bombs without explosive for war reserves as you claim in paragraph 12 of your report -- no, it's a different report. It's 65 ter 08347, 08347.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be the last question for today. Exhibit P2318.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 88 in the Serbian, I think, and in the hard copy, it's page 84. In English we need page 97. Look at paragraph 12.1. You say here that Pretis factory was developing an aerosol air-bomb, the first 50 bombs were completed, so and so, et cetera. Can you please look at this paragraph and then tell us where did you get this information that Pretis used to deliver bombs without explosives?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that we are misunderstanding each other. In 1998, the Yugoslav army introduced the aerosol bomb into its range of weaponry, which began to be developed in Pretis before the war. I have the standard at home, the military standard, in order to pass the FAB 275 aerosol bomb. And what you're seeing here where it says, the Pretis factory developed the aerosol fuel-air-bomb, the first 50 bombs were made in 1990 and the next phase was due to be concluded in 1991-1992, followed by serial production. We are talking about FAB 275. I have photographs of those bombs, FAB 275s, and these bombs, 24 of them, are currently in the depot of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They need to be destroyed because they pose a danger to the lives of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are not talking about FAB 250.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But those that were hitting Sarajevo, you said that they were of the 100 and 250 type; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are rocket-assisted aerosol bombs, 250, modified or improvised, and they were the ones that were dropping on Sarajevo in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's it for today. I wonder, Dr. Zecevic, if you have been informed that tomorrow we will be sitting in the morning, starting at 9.00. Does it cause you a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it does create problems for me. If you look, I have been walking or standing for five hours. I should be fit. But I will make it. Yes, I will be here tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate very much your cooperation. We will be sitting in the same manner tomorrow, as we are today. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of February, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
